title: Namo hiraṇyabāhave: homage to the golden one
theme: A litany of homage to Śiva as golden, as the husband of Ambikā and Umā, and as lord of all creatures.

words.role: subject of the nominal sentence (‘homage [be] to …’)

words.context: Sāyaṇa: the arm stands for every limb, «सुवर्गमयकृत्स्नशरीरयुक्ताय» — whose whole body is golden; Bhāskara: «हिरण्याभरणालङ्कृतबाहवे» — whose arms are adorned with gold
The anonymous commentator takes varṇa as the letters of the Veda, as hard to come by as gold: «दुर्लभा वर्णा वेदाक्षराणि यस्मादुत्पद्यन्ते स हिरण्यवर्णः»

words.meaning: to the one of golden form
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «हिरण्यरूपाय तेजोमयाय» — made of radiance
Sāyaṇa: «हिरण्यपतयेऽस्मदीयहिरण्यपालकाय» — the guardian of our gold; Bhāskara: «हितरमणीयानामर्थानां स्वामिने» — lord of things beneficial and delightful
Sāyaṇa: «अम्बिका जगन्माता पार्वती» — Ambikā is Pārvatī, mother of the world
Sāyaṇa: «तस्या एवाम्बिकाया ब्रह्मविद्यात्मको देह उमाशब्देनोच्यते» — Umā is Ambikā’s own form as knowledge of Brahman
The anonymous commentator: «पशूनामाब्रह्मस्तम्बपर्यन्तानां पतिर्नायकः पशुपतिस्तस्मै» — lord of all creatures from Brahmā down to a blade of grass

sandhi.rule: -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced sound: namaḥ + hiraṇyabāhave → namo hiraṇyabāhave.

A final e stays before a, which is elided and marked by the avagraha (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)): hiraṇyapataye ’mbikāpataye. Before u the e becomes ay (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः)) and the y is dropped (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)), leaving the vowels apart: ambikāpataya umāpataye.

morphology.note: The neuter noun namas, ‘a bow’, with the dative of the one honoured: namo hiraṇyabāhave, ‘homage to the golden-armed’. The verb ‘be’ is understood. Bhāskara notes that the closing namo namaḥ is not mere repetition, since each carries its own accent: «नैतद्द्विर्वचनं द्वितीयस्याप्युदात्तत्वात्».

Ambikā and Umā are two names of the same goddess. Bhāskara explains the doubling either as respect, Umā being the name dear to the seer Vāmadeva, «आदरार्थं पुनर्वचनम् उमाशब्दप्रियत्वाद् वामदेवस्य», or as two states of one power.

translation.literal: Homage to the golden-armed, to the golden-coloured, to the one of golden form, to the lord of gold, to the husband of Ambikā, to the husband of Umā, to the lord of creatures — homage, homage.
translation.readable: Homage to him whose arms are gold, whose colour is gold, whose form is gold, the lord of gold; to the husband of Ambikā, the husband of Umā, the lord of all creatures — homage, and again homage.

syntax: One nominal sentence: namaḥ (‘homage [be]’) followed by seven datives, each a compound naming the one honoured, and closed by a doubled namo namaḥ.

ambiguities.note: Literally ‘golden-coloured’. The anonymous commentator reads varṇa as the letters of the Veda, which come from him and are as rare as gold to those who have not studied under a teacher; Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara do not take it so.

‘Lord of gold’: guardian of the worshipper’s wealth for Sāyaṇa, keeper of the nine treasures for the anonymous commentator («हिरण्योपलक्षितनवनिधिपालकत्वाद्धिरण्यपतिस्तस्मै»), lord of what is good and delightful for Bhāskara.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A yajus litany of 45 syllables in one line, without metrical division.

beginner: This is a short chant of homage. Seven times it bows to the same god, each time with a new title. Three titles call him golden: golden-armed, golden-coloured, golden in form, and a fourth makes him lord of gold. Two name him as husband of the goddess, by two of her names, Ambikā and Umā. The last calls him Paśupati, lord of all creatures. The old commentators explain each title differently. One says the golden arm stands for a whole golden body; another hears in ‘golden-coloured’ the letters of the Veda, as precious and hard to obtain as gold. The chant ends ‘homage, homage’, the doubled bow that also closes many other Vedic chants to Rudra. It states its praise; it does not say what saying it brings.
analogy: Like a row of lamps lit one after another before the same image: each title is a new light on one figure.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It offers homage to one figure under seven names: golden-armed, golden-coloured, of golden form, lord of gold, husband of Ambikā, husband of Umā, lord of creatures; and it ends with a doubled homage.

commentary.q: Who is honoured, and how is the mantra used?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator introduces it as another mantra to the same deity as the preceding Īśāna mantra, «पुनरपि तद्देवताकं मन्त्रान्तरमाह», and ends with homage to Śiva. Sāyaṇa, for whom this is his anuvāka 18 and the third of three on Rudra, says the mantras of the three are known in the manuals as the Tvaritarudra: «अनेनानुवाकत्रयेणोक्तानां मन्त्राणां त्वरितरुद्राख्या मन्त्रकल्पेषु प्रसिद्धा». Their use, he adds, is as a supplement to the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya, to be learned from the ritual manuals: «तद्विनियोगस्तु रुद्राध्यायजपशेषत्वेन कल्पेषु द्रष्टव्यः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator takes paśu, ‘creature’, in the widest sense, all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, and cites a verse: «ब्रह्माद्याः स्तम्बपर्यन्ताः पशवः परिकीर्तिताः». For Umā he cites a verse he attributes to the poets: «उ मेति मात्रा तपसे निषिद्धा पश्चादुमाख्यां सुमुखी जगाम».

commentary.q: Ambikā and Umā: two names, one goddess?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara offers two readings. The doubling may be for respect, the name Umā being dear to the seer Vāmadeva; or Ambikā is the supreme power as it brings forth the world, «सर्वविकल्पोन्मेषवती परा शक्तिः», and Umā the same power at the world’s dissolution, called by a name equal to the praṇava: «प्रणवपर्यायेण उमाशब्देनोच्यते».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The three commentaries present differ on the meaning of single titles, not on doctrine.

contemporary.text: A litany says the same thing seven ways. Its point is not information but attention: each new name turns the mind to the same figure from another side. Naming something carefully, again and again, is how attention is held. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Four of the seven titles mention gold. What might gold stand for in a prayer?
reflect.deeper: The commentators give each title a different sense. Does a litany need one fixed meaning for each name, or does it work by allowing several?
reflect.practice: Read the seven titles aloud slowly, pausing after each, and notice what image each one raises.

references.text: Several of these titles, beginning namo hiraṇyabāhave, also occur in the Śrī Rudram of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (TS 4.5.2), which this edition cannot yet cite as a parallel; see the site’s Śrī Rudram edition.
Sāyaṇa comments on this mantra as his anuvāka 18, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara as his anuvāka 18; the edition’s concordance maps both correctly here.

flags.note: The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text prints only the end of the line (from …पतयेऽम्बिकापतय), the rest being given in its commentary; the collation lists the gap for review. The base and the Tirupati e-text agree on the full line.
The readings of hiraṇyavarṇa (the letters of the Veda) and of Ambikā and Umā as two states of one power are the commentators’, not stated in the text.
